Whole-repository assessment · 7 September 2026

city-digital-twin, assessed at af7d718

An agent-based microsimulation of Newcastle, New South Wales — twelve modes, each physically simulated on the real roads and timetables and scored against its own real-life ridership. This is a reading of one commit, four commits past the previous report of the same day, and the first pass to measure the synthetic demand itself against the observations the package already holds.

the one-paragraph verdict

The instrument is sound; the day it simulates is not the day Newcastle has

Four commits separate this reading from this morning's. They closed the five defects that had blocked every launch, so for the first time the issue gate, the toolchain gate and the launcher agreed and an arm is running in family F30 as this is written. What this pass adds is not another read of the code but a read of the demand: the synthetic population and the synthetic day were measured against observations the package has held all along — the census joint tables, the 2011 journey-to-work flows, the hourly count profile, the Opal tap times. They disagree in ways no run can repair. The synthetic day puts 19.6 % of departures after 20:00 against 6.2 % observed and 6.4 % after midnight against none, because tours are stacked one after another on assumed durations; a third of the taxi excess is night trips the model manufactures. The public-transport day is inverted against the Hunter's taps — a school peak the model does not have, an evening the observed bus does not serve. Income and occupation are drawn independently of age while income scales every person's marginal utility of money, and car-less households are lone-person 36 % of the time against 65 % nationally. Commute destinations match the job map within half a point, but the flows do not: own-LGA commuting runs 7 to 26 points under the journey-to-work table and the 12.8 % of workers who leave the region do not exist. These are the causes GOAL.md's loop tells a session to find before it moves a constant, and every one of them is in the build layer before MATSim starts. The engineering findings of the morning's report stand where the four commits did not touch them: 24 of its 95 findings are closed, 46 still open.

What was read, by whom, and what the ratings mean

Phase 1 ran the three collectors. Phases 2–7 ran as six independent reviewers — one code reviewer for the six areas, one performance analyst, one historian, one document reviewer, one field researcher, one factor researcher — each reading only its lane and returning a file the writer merged. The demand-synthesis measurements were made by the session itself before the report opened, on the F29 demand and the F28 gate's trips table, and are labelled measured this pass wherever they appear.

The rating rubric

Five dimensions per area, 1–5: correctness (does it do what its docstring claims, with the failure it names), clarity (can a reader who did not write it follow it), testability (is there a check that would catch its regression), efficiency (does it do the work once), adherence (the hard constraints in .claude/CLAUDE.md). A 5 needs two pieces of evidence for; a 1 needs two against. Ratings are never averaged across areas.

What happened, in twelve lines

  1. 10 August - the repository opens with one commit called 'proposal' and, within nine hours, three merged pull requests: P1's 182-file hashed data package, P2's 157,678-link MATSim network with all 15 GTFS feeds mapped, and P3's tour-based demand. None of it had been run, and all three PRs say so.
  2. 11 August - the first attempt to execute MATSim refuses to load all thirty assembled run-input sets. PR #4 fixes three defects, measures the first cost curve (9.8 / 29.9 / ~64 s an iteration) and records that thirteen of the sixty-seven calibration targets can identify nothing.
  3. 15-16 August - PR #38's rebuild: a typed-in OSM harvest box had clipped 87 core SA1s out of the road network. Core SA1s without a road node fall 99 to 4, the config is emitted from 297 declared registry fields, and family F1 produces the project's first completed 1000-iteration arm.
  4. 18-21 August - ride pairing is built and immediately measured starved (0.104% of ride trips share an OD with a household car trip); escort binding and census age structure repair the demand; every person-transport mode becomes physical (F3); the walk wedge is found and repaired (F4) - the last family to date whose arms ran to their declared horizon.
  5. 20-21 August - process hardens after five of six stacked pull requests never reach main: PRs target main only, direct commits to main are banned, and the session's one PR opens at /handoff. The sixth and last direct commit lands seventeen minutes before the rule merges; there has not been one since.
  6. 24-25 August - SUMO is descoped by recorded decision, the signals run stack is pinned by sha256, and the all-modes batch (signals, taxi, crossings, dwell) is built inert with byte-identical run inputs, then activated as family F6. The first gate stop follows the same day.
  7. 25 August - two documentation PRs answer the drift the front door had accumulated: check_doc_currency.py pins every live-state number to its artefact (#83), and the light rail's published -63% 'error' is retracted against a target the fit itself marks unscorable (#85).
  8. 27-29 August - the gate loop starts firing on the twenty-percent bar. PR #95 fixes three yardsticks that had been wrong at every iteration - one counted another city's light rail stop - and corrects four of its own session's conclusions in the same body.
  9. 30 August - the busiest day of the project: 87 commits, six comparability families (F15-F20), 31 record sections, a demand rebuilt twice, and the document restructure into GOAL.md, a one-page generated board and thirteen position pages, so a session reads 600 lines instead of a 13,000-line record.
  10. 31 August - 2 September - public transport is priced at the published Opal fare, then bike stress, parking search time and income-scaled money sensitivity enter the model. Bus comes inside its band at the F22 gate, the first of the twelve modes ever to; the results store makes the run lifecycle automatic.
  11. 3-7 September - the first whole-repository assessment lodges 26 issues and the next PR closes fourteen without a run; destination choice is constrained at both ends and the iteration is cut from 384 s to a median 260 s; F25 falsifies the demand-side cause for ride; a declared driver must own a car (F26); a global qsim wait strands every non-chain mode (F27, citable for nothing); and at the F28 gate car reads +6.6%, inside the band at a gate for the first time - with ride still -42.8% and seven modes past the bar.
  12. 7 September - the third report finds the 67/143 holdout informing the count targets and 34 defects CI could not see; PR #152 closes 29 (heavy share 0.0652 -> 0.1120, counts on one basis, three blind checks widened, --stop scoped to one arm) and files the five that block a launch; the session branch rules on all five, opens F30 on the escort listener's draw order, has its launch refused by a toolchain gate that was green on a missing run stack, fixes the gate, and launches the first F30 arm at 15:08 - running at iteration 17, no run since F4 having reached its horizon.

code quality

Six areas, read in order, each with its blind spot declared

Build layer

Raw downloads -> city extract adapters -> src/build layer builders (network, population, chains, plans) -> city builders (corridor, validation targets, scenario schedules) -> build_matsim_run_inputs.py assembles one directory per scenario x day type, emitting the MATSim config from the registry through param_config. Every value is meant to arrive through registry.load(); build_manifest.py closes the loop by hashing every artefact and joining it to a provenance record. The layer is deterministic by seed 20260810 and by det_io for byte-stable gzip; the two places that bypass det_io are the two findings below.

Testability. Zero of 22 src/build modules is imported by any test except hts_purpose.py (test_one_map_one_order). The pure primitives (shape_tools, det_io, osm_parse, gtfs_tools) are importable and side-effect free and could be unit-tested in seconds; the builders are main()-shaped with module-level registry loads and pandas reads, testable only against the 2.3 GiB package through check_package.py. The nearest_node ring bug (#52) and the imputation fallbacks (#16) are exactly the class a ten-line synthetic test would have caught.

Run harness

run.py resolves the registry through the overlay chain (scenario, day, run tag, env, --set), refuses an unlaunchable configuration before the JVM (toolchain gate, issue gate, telemetry barrier), builds the run directory under results/raw, emits the config, starts CitysimControler and a gate watcher that runs report_mode_ridership at every RUN.gate.interval_iterations; close_out writes _run.json with a completion value and results_store mirrors the record files to results/processed and trims the raw cache to RUN.storage.raw_cap_gb. A dead run must state its cause from its own log (run_failure.py).

Analysis and calibration

A finished run is turned into _metrics.json by extract_metrics, scored by fit.py against the calibration split only, summarised, indexed and drawn. report_mode_ridership is both the operator's table and the gate watcher's verdict (it writes the gate JSON the watcher reads). calibrate.py searches over registry keys and, with --execute, is meant to launch a run per candidate through run_matsim. The measurement layer reads CAL.* fields and is excluded from the hardcoding gate's report-only rule by name.

Contract and checks

The registry resolver is the single input surface: values from cities/<city>/registry, overlays that may only set existing fields inside their sweep, env and --set. Every strict load runs the intrinsic rules. param_config emits tool configs from bindings and proves reach by nudging each field. check_hardcoding is the CI gate at 0 over five questions; check_city holds a city to the generated contract; check_doc_currency/shape pin the living documents; check_city_agnostic builds a fixture city and asserts differences.

Acquisition and data

Fetch adapters download named resources into data/raw with a provenance list (URL, sha256, licence, retrieval date); extract adapters clip them to the study area whose extent is derived from the LGA boundary; reader_shapes.py is the only place the framework meets the published column vocabulary. build_manifest joins every artefact to its record. The ODbL/CC-BY split is declared by glob in city.json.

MATSim extensions

CitysimControler.assemble registers every custom config group before parsing (an unmaterialised module fails MATSim's check), loads the scenario, pins activities to usable links, then installs each extension only when its declared representation asks for it. Extensions act at fixed seams: BeforeMobsim on stable selected plans (ride pairing, taxi fleet), replanning (escort coherence, gated mode choice), the qsim departure chain in an explicit order (household car wait, netsim, joint ride, teleport), and event handlers that accumulate and emit deferred money/score events at AfterMobsim. The signals stack adds SCATS and tram priority controllers in src/java_signals.

The Opal comparator is bus only. The journey-to-work table is 2011; TfNSW publishes 2016 and 2021 flows at travel zone. None of this is a run result, and the F30 arm in flight will not change it: all of it is in the demand before MATSim starts.

simulator performance

Where an iteration goes, and what the arm in flight is doing

Phase 3 of /project-report at HEAD af7d718, 7 September 2026 ~17:10. Every figure is read from SCRATCH/metrics/performance.json (each run's own output/stopwatch.csv, telemetry.jsonl, _config.json, matsim.log MemoryObserver lines, dump byte walk; collected 17:00), from a run directory's own files (the in-flight arm's _progress.json, stopwatch.csv, telemetry.jsonl, _meta.json, matsim.log head/tail), from a file:line at HEAD, from the registry, or from one Get-Process / Win32_Process listing taken at 17:07. Figures carried from the previous pass (419b0da, this morning) are marked 'previous pass' and were re-checked against the unchanged artefact they came from. Nothing is estimated; a measurement that would need a run says 'unmeasured - needs a probe arm'. Nothing was modified, compiled or launched; no matsim.log was read whole.

findingNo producing script records its wall time, and the one that records anything writes it into a hashed artefact, so a byte-identical rebuild changes a manifest hash for a reason unrelated to the data. The cost of reproducing the ~2.3 GiB package is unknown.
where the timing would be writtena per-layer sidecar <layer>/_timing.json (script, argv, started, wall_s, host) written by every producing script through one helper in src/build, never inside a hashed report; plus a non-hashed build_wall_s column in MANIFEST.csv that check_manifest.py accepts. Moving gtfs_seconds / mapping_seconds into the sidecar closes the hash instability at the same time.

The 250-iteration verdict

Reachable inside a day on the machine as it stands, and not the constraint. At the last completed gate's own measured median - 258.5 s an iteration on the F28 arm (aborted_20260907T030352_300it_25pct, 25 %, 16 threads, 100 iterations timed, p90 282, 27,657 s to iteration 100) - 250 iterations is 64,625 s = 18.0 h of plain iterations, ~18.5-19 h with the milestone dumps at 0, 1, 100 and 200; the F30 arm's own digest, at its in-flight 375 s median, puts the same horizon at 26 h and 300 iterations at 31 h (106,136 s remaining at iteration 17). Either fits the one-arm-at-a-time rule and GOAL.md requirement 8's horizon. What would halve it is not on the table: the iteration is 62-65 % mobsim, 19-21 % replanning and 13-15 % prepareForMobsim, our own listeners are 1-3 s of it, and the mobsim is measured to saturate (2.4x the threads bought 6 % of it); the fraction is fixed by the 1 September directive and 1 % is ruled unusable; the untried levers that touch no result are the heap (40 g against a 13.3 GiB live set, above the compressed-oops line, never probed with a GC log) and the machine itself - a stray one-core python from yesterday's report session and a foreground load since 16:08 sit beside the JVM, and F30's step from 287 to 386 s an iteration coincides with both the model's own growth in car and ride departures and that load. Halving 258.5 s would need ~130 s that no measured lever offers. The real risk to requirement 8 is unchanged from this morning: no arm has been allowed past iteration 100 in six consecutive families, so convergence and the innovation-off tail's cost remain unmeasured.

the field

44 comparable projects, 12 platforms, and the rung nobody occupies

What the comparison says

  • No project in the survey publishes a per-mode fit for every mode it simulates. The highest published rung is transit ridership by operator or station group (MWCOG Gen3, PSRC SoundCast, MATSim-NYC, CMAP), and every one of those is a skim-and-assignment model, not agent-simulated public transport. The twelve-mode per-mode bar this project set has no published precedent to be judged against.
  • The agency reports that publish the whole ladder with numbers accept far looser fits than this project's gates: MWCOG Gen3 calls 43% RMSE on 8,069 counts, +/-9% on transit by mode and +/-20% on station groups 'reasonable' and ready for production; PSRC deliberately under-fits to keep sensitivity. A 10% bar per mode and a 20% stop bar are stricter than any acceptance standard found.
  • Physical completeness and published fit are inversely related in the field: SimMobility, POLARIS, ETH's 2012 Singapore model and this project simulate PT, freight, pricing (and here signals) physically and publish few or no fit figures; the models with full validation tables hand demand to an aggregate assignment.
  • The 25% sample is at the top of the field and has a published rationale: ETH Singapore chose 25% 'to prevent artefacts when simulating public transport', scaling the smallest bus from 72 to 21 seats; Leipzig, Kelheim and Montreal run at 25%, most open MATSim scenarios at 1-10%. The ~22 h arm cost is the price every 25% PT-physical model pays.
  • Calibrated MATSim city models report mode-share fit in percentage points of share (Berlin v6 MAE <0.5 pp; GTA RMSE 4.07 pp; Tyne and Wear <=3.5 pp; Dhaka accepts a 19 pp gap on NMT). This board scores relative deviation per mode, which is why taxi reads +161% on a 1.6 pp gap and ferry -68.7% on a 0.1 pp gap - the field's yardstick would call several of the 'STOP' modes close.
  • Explicit signals are rare: SimMobility's short-term level and TRANSIMS model them; Berlin v6 states it does not; ETH Singapore could not because the operator's signal plans were proprietary - exactly the SCATS-offset obstacle this project records. Implementing SCATS as its published algorithm is a field first as far as this library sees.
  • The generative and LLM lane has stopped producing: two further rounds this pass found nothing new that validates against observation. The entries that do close the loop are not LLM agents at all - GTA (personas into SUMO, scored on Berlin counts) and the UCLA generative models (Deep Activity Model, DeepCAM; scored on PeMS detectors) - and the independent evaluation of the pure-LLM cities finds their trips spatially unrealistic.
  • Australia is unchanged: Melbourne (AToM and its Suburban Rail Loop extension) and Bendigo remain the only calibrated agent-based city models found; nothing agent-based exists for NSW, and the state's own 'digital twin' is a visualisation platform with an AI congestion predictor, not a travel model.

What others do best that this project lacks

whowhat they dowhy it matters here
MWCOG Gen3 (ActivitySim, Washington DC)Publishes each validation number beside the acceptance standard it is judged against (FDOT/FSUTMS: +/-5% VMT areawide, +/-9% transit by mode, +/-20% station groups, RMSE by volume group).This project's 10% and 20% gates are its own; a published external standard per observation type would let the board say whether a mode is close by the field's yardstick, not only by ours.
PSRC SoundCast (DaySim + Emme)Reports counts by facility type and time period, screenlines, boardings by operator and by route, and says where it under-fits on purpose.The board reports one deviation per mode; SoundCast's layout is the template for a per-mode ladder that keeps the count and boarding comparisons visible alongside the share.
MATSim Open Berlin v6 (TU Berlin VSP)Closed-form ASC update from survey shares that converges in about five runs, checked three ways (survey, routing-API speeds, count stations).Each arm here costs ~22 h; an automated share-driven ASC step between arms would spend that cost on one adjustment per mode rather than on a hand-picked lever.
Deep Activity Model / DeepCAM (UCLA Mobility Lab)A nationally trained activity-chain generator fine-tuned on a thin regional survey, with household coordination, scored on corridor detectors.The Hunter HTS sample is thin; a chain generator trained on the national survey and tuned locally is the derivation route GOAL.md requirement 6 asks for, and household-coupled chains are what the ride/escort lane is reconstructing by hand.
ETH MATSim Singapore 2012 (Erath et al.)Bus lanes as parallel mode-restricted links, per-door dwell-time models, and a stated reason for the 25% sample (PT capacity artefacts, bus 72 -> 21 seats).Bus is +65% here; the dwell and bus-lane treatment are supply-side levers not yet in the registry, and the capacity-scaling rationale is the one to cite for the 25% directive.
Tyne and Wear MATSim (Newcastle University, UK)Validates the calibrated base against a real bridge closure using hourly sensor flows.A disruption the network actually experienced (a Stockton Bridge or Hunter Expressway closure) is a validation the holdout targets cannot give and that the count stations (#82) could.
Brussels cellphone-matrix MATSim (VUB)Builds and validates a MATSim demand from aggregated cellphone OD matrices with no household survey.External and visitor demand here is derived from the 2011 journey-to-work flow; an aggregated mobile-network matrix for the Hunter would replace a fifteen-year-old proxy.
Dhaka BRT MATSim (Leeds)Wires a jointly estimated RP-SP choice model into MATSim scoring and prices a service that does not exist yet, then states which observed gaps it accepted and why.S1-S6 price a light rail and a shuttle that the HTS never observed; the RP-SP-into-scoring pattern is how a counterfactual mode gets a defensible ASC.

The full ledger

layerfactorwhat the research saysmagnitudehow the leaders do itstatusproof at HEADwhat it would move
AResidential location (fixed from census)Residential self-selection is a measured but minority share of the built-environment effect: disentangling it by housing type in one study put self-selection at 15.2%, 30.7%, 18.5% and 5.9% of the total impact on vehicle kilometres travelled for the four housing types examined, and the effect is modest for the elderly and large for younger adults. The built-environment side remains the Ewing-Cervero meta-analysis, with every 5D elasticity inelastic. A residence fixed from the census therefore carries most of the built-environment effect and mis-states only the self-selected minority. srcliterature: self-selection 6-31% of the total built-environment effect on VKT, varying by housing type; the remainder is the location itselfUrbanSim-class land-use models re-choose residence; ActivitySim, CT-RAMP, MATSim and eqasim all take residence from the synthetic population and never re-choose it during a run.INsrc/build/build_population.py:281 - households placed on SA1 residence marginals via READERS.residence_marginals(sa1); no relocation choice exists anywhere under src/Nothing directly: residence is an input, not a lever. The measured demand defects this pass are downstream of it (income, vehicles, schedule), not in it.
AWorkplace locationWorkplace location is a calibrated long-term choice in every activity-based practice: ActivitySim samples commute distances from regional distributions and selects zones to match them under land-use compatibility, then validates residence-to-work flows against the census commuting-flow table and the mandatory trip-length frequency distribution; where attractions are more reliable than the impedance the practice is doubly constrained (shadow-priced) so that both worker totals and job totals are held. The output check the field uses is the county-to-county (here LGA-to-LGA) flow table, not the mean distance. src needs researchunknown as a coefficient: the practice benchmark is an origin-destination flow table (census journey-to-work) and a trip-length distribution, not a central tendencyActivitySim and CT-RAMP run a shadow-priced work location choice validated against census commuting flows; MATSim scenarios assign workplaces in the demand builder and hold them fixed.INsrc/build/build_zone_attractions.py:43-45 (D.attraction.job_weight_by_category, D.attraction.purpose_weight) weight work attraction per zone; src/build/build_activity_chains.py:465 calibrate_decay solves the draw to the HTS mean journey distance per purpose and LGA. Measured this pass on the F29 demand: the top work SA2s agree with JTW 2011 within 0.5 points (Newcastle-Cooks Hill 8.4% vs 8.3%, Hamilton-Broadmeadow 5.5% vs 5.6%) - the attraction side is right; the flow side is on the distance-decay rowHeavy rail +295.1%: the over-boarding in #98 is long multi-leg rail trips of outer-LGA residents, an inter-LGA flow excess of exactly the shape the own-LGA shortfall (7-26 points) produces. Workplace attractions are not the cause; the flow structure is.
AVehicle ownership per householdHousehold car ownership is one of the strongest single predictors of mode: an increase in car ownership raises the probability of commuting by car and depresses active and transit modes, with a reported elasticity of -2.643 for the substitution of active modes. Income, household size, distance to centre, accessibility to shops/services/employment and intersection density are the dominant explanatory variables. srcliterature: elasticity of active-mode use with respect to car ownership approximately -2.6; income and household size the leading sociodemographic driversActivitySim/CT-RAMP run an explicit auto-ownership choice model calibrated to observed auto sufficiency; MATSim scenarios usually take vehicles from the synthetic population and enforce availability through chain-based mode constraints rather than re-choosing ownership.INB.population.vehicle_roster = census (cities/newcastle/registry/B_demand.json); src/java/citysim/HouseholdVehicleRoster.java bound at src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:471-472 so a household drives only the cars the census gives it. But the COUNT is drawn at src/build/build_population.py:296 (veh = norm(m['vehicles'])) and :322 (nv = rng.choice(veh_vals, p=veh)) from G34 alone, independent of household size, composition and incomeThis mechanism moved car to +6.6% at F28. Measured this pass on the F29 demand: car-less households are the wrong households - 36.0% of zero-car households are lone-person against 65.3% nationally (ABS Transport: Census 2021), and 91.3% of the 29,423 adults in them hold a licence - so the car-less quarter of trips (9.123) that carries bike +157.3%, bus +65.0% and ride -42.8% is made by people who would not be car-less.
AVehicle type (EV, e-bike)The e-bike evidence is now meta-analysed: across experimental studies, access to an e-bike adds about 5 km of daily travel and raises e-bike mode share by about 26 percentage points, while car use falls by about 2.4 km a day (a 10% drop in car mode share); single controlled trials report car share falling 21%, and older meta-studies put e-bike-for-car substitution at 43% of trips and 63% of mileage. The effect is context-dependent: where cycling is already high the e-bike substitutes conventional cycling; where it is low it draws from car and public transport. (Figures are abstract-level; the full text was not retrievable this pass.) srcliterature: +5 km/day travelled and +26 pp e-bike share with e-bike access; car -2.4 km/day (~-10% car share); substitution 43% of car trips in earlier synthesesMATSim's bicycle contrib carries an e-bike as a vehicle type with its own speed and gradient response; no production city model draws an e-bike or EV ownership decision - both enter as a share of the fleet.OUTgrep -riE 'e-bike|ebike|electric_vehicle' under src/, cities/newcastle/build and cities/newcastle/registry matches nothing but analysis-file EVent tokens; the vehicle roster carries no drivetrain or e-assist attribute, and B.bike.speed_ms is one 4.2 m/s for every cyclistNothing on the current board. An e-bike share would raise feasible cycling range and speed, which points the wrong way against bike at +157.3%.
ALicence holdingLicence holding among people under 35 has fallen across Australia, the UK, the US, Canada and much of Europe: TfNSW reports 65.4% of 16-20 year olds licensed in 2017, 8.3 points below 2001 and 8.1 below 2009, with the proportion licensed at age 30 also declining cohort on cohort. The travel-behaviour consequence named is a greater reliance on getting a lift, especially in wealthy suburbs and high-car-ownership families, and more public transport, walking and cycling in less wealthy areas. srcliterature: 16-20 licence rate 65.4% (2017 NSW), down ~8 points on 2001; effect is a shift toward being a car passenger and toward PT/active modesActivitySim/CT-RAMP treat licence holding inside the auto-ownership and person-type models; MATSim scenarios encode it as a person attribute gating car as a chain-based mode.INsrc/build/build_population.py:62 - LICENCE_RATE = CFG.get('B.population.licence_rate_by_age_band'), measured from the published count and applied per LGA (:63-65, licence_rates_by_age_lga.csv); DECISIONS.md 9.131Directly relevant to ride at -42.8%: the literature says the licence decline shows up as lifts. Licence rates are measured here, so the ride shortfall is not licence supply - but 91.3% of adults in zero-car households hold a licence (measured this pass), which is the vehicles draw, not the licence draw.
APublic-transport passes / concessionsA smartcard natural experiment on Dutch fares separates pass holders from single-ticket users: passengers on a monthly or annual subscription have the highest travel frequency per origin-destination pair per week - almost twice that of single-ticket users - and the estimated fare elasticities split cleanly between the frequent-user products (pay-as-you-go, student and subscription) and the occasional ones (end-of-month and single tickets). A pass converts the fare from a per-trip price to a zero marginal cost, and the behavioural response is the frequency, not the mode. srcliterature: subscription holders travel about 2x as often per OD pair as single-ticket users; fare elasticity differs by product classActivitySim/CT-RAMP carry a per-person fare class or pass flag into the cost term; MATSim fare handlers (as here) price per trip and per day-cap, so a pass has to be expressed as a zero marginal fare for the holder.PARTIALC.vot.concession_factor read at src/build/build_params.py:54, and A.fare.senior_per_fare_cap / daily_cap_senior / daily_cap_child / child_min_age / child_max_age / senior_min_age declared in cities/newcastle/registry/A_supply.json and priced by src/java/citysim/PtFareChargeHandler.java (bound at src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:401-403); no pass PRODUCT (zero marginal fare) is representedBus +65.0% and heavy_rail +295.1% both over-carry; a pass makes PT cheaper at the margin, so this is not the lever that closes them. The literature's 2x frequency for pass holders bears on the school and senior markets the Opal profile shows and the model lacks.
ABicycle ownershipOwnership is high and use is low, and the two are only weakly coupled: the National Cycling Participation Survey (2011-2019) finds more than half of Australian households own at least one bicycle while cycling is 1.4% of daily travel; Melbourne apartment households own 0.86 bicycles on average, off-street bicycle parking more than doubles the odds a household owns one, and the correlation between household bicycles and regional cycling use is 0.238. Ownership is male, younger, more educated and higher-income; renting, apartment living and foreign origin reduce it. srcliterature: >50% of households own a bicycle against 1.4% cycling mode share (NCPS); 0.86 bikes per apartment household; ownership-use correlation 0.24ActivitySim implementations gate bike by a household bicycle flag where the survey carries it; MATSim scenarios (as here) draw an availability rate per person and let mode choice decide use; no production model estimates an ownership choice.PARTIALB.population.bike_available_rate (0.493, source literature) read at src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:62 and drawn per person at :371 with B.population.bike_min_age (:213); availability exists, no ownership decision does, and the draw is independent of age beyond the minimum, sex, income and dwellingBike is +157.3%, the second-worst mode. The literature now says ownership (>50% of households) and use (1.4% of travel) are only weakly coupled (r = 0.24), so a 0.49 availability rate applied uniformly is the single most direct dial on bike volume and the ownership-use gap is the mechanism the model lacks.

Measured this pass on the F29 demand: 19.6% of synthetic core legs depart after 20:00 and 6.4% after midnight against 6.2% and 0% in the observed light-vehicle profile (551 station-years); home-bound legs 27.2% after 20:00; legs per person 0-4 1.37, 65-74 3.03 (26.1% immobile) against 8-12% one-day immobility in the survey literature. The stable ~81 min/day travel budget is the literature check that has not been run.
BJoint household decisionsJoint and partially joint travel is a material share of household tours: partially joint tours - where one or more passengers is dropped off or picked up mid-tour - make up close to 14% of all tour types in metropolitan areas, and households with more than one student at the same school very commonly serve them on one car tour. srcliterature: partially joint tours ~14% of all tour typesCT-RAMP models joint tours explicitly (participation, party composition, destination); ActivitySim carries the same joint-tour chain; MATSim has no native joint-tour construct and scenarios add it as a contrib or in the demand builder.INsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:218 (B.activity.joint_tour_purposes) with B.activity.joint_tour_passenger_ratio (0.3503, derived) and B.ride.joint_coherence_rate; src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:488-490 binds JointRideEngine as a QSim componentRide is -42.8%. The literature's ~14% partially-joint tour share and the 70% household share of lifts are the yardsticks for whether the bound-trip population is the right size before pairing is blamed.
BEscort of childrenEscorting is modelled in practice as a nested choice: school tours split into outbound and inbound half-tours, each with pure escort / ridesharing / no escort and up to three household chauffeurs. Significant determinants are the chauffeur's employment status, age and flexibility at work, the child's age, household characteristics and the relative distances between home, school and workplace; mothers working longer hours and further from home are less likely to chauffeur. srcliterature: three escort alternatives per half-tour, up to three candidate chauffeurs; chauffeur work hours and job distance are the leading determinantsCT-RAMP and ActivitySim implement a dedicated school-escort model with chauffeur assignment; MATSim carries no escort construct natively.INsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:177 (B.activity.escort_binding_enabled) with escort_requires_licence, escort_binding_scope, escort_excludes_ride (src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:200); src/java/citysim/EscortCoherenceListener.java bound at src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:456-458, its draw now in TreeMap order (EscortCoherenceListener.java:94-100, 9.151, family F30)Escort is the demand-side source of car-passenger legs, so it bears on ride at -42.8%. Education tours are under-generated ~40% (measured this pass: HE 5.7% of legs against 9.6% HTS), so the escort pool that feeds ride is itself short.
BTelework / work-from-homeTelework reduces commuting and business trips, most clearly for full-time teleworkers, but the effect on TOTAL distance is mixed and design-dependent: rebound effects (extra non-work trips) and residential relocation to longer commutes offset part of the saving, and one-worker households increase total travel - particularly by car - while two-worker households show no significant increase. srcliterature: commute trips reduced; total distance effect ambiguous with documented rebound and relocation offsetsActivitySim implementations added post-pandemic work-from-home models as a person-level choice feeding the daily activity pattern; MATSim scenarios usually encode it by removing work activities from a share of plans.OUTgrep -riE 'telework|work_from_home|wfh' under src/, cities/newcastle/build and cities/newcastle/registry matches only a comment at src/analyse/measure_demographic_modes.py:316 and the sweep_basis note on B.activity.p_mandatory (census night 19.2% WFH bounds the sweep, sets nothing); every employed person commutes at P_MANDATORY 0.78 (src/build/build_activity_chains.py:159) with no per-person attribute. Measured this pass on the F29 demand: HW 18.6% of legs against 14.0% HTS commute share (work tours per employed person 0.71 vs ~0.63 implied); ABS August 2025 puts 36% of employed people usually working from homeCommute over-generated 10-25% inflates the peak where bus (+65.0%) and heavy_rail (+295.1%) over-carry and car sits at +6.6%. This is the largest OUT factor on the two worst PT deviations, and the literature says the commute reduction is the one unambiguous telework effect.
BDay-type differences (weekday, Saturday, Sunday)Weekend travel has a different shape, not just a different volume: the sharp early-morning and mid-afternoon weekday peaks are absent on the weekend day because so few trips are to and from work, and social-recreational and personal-business travel spread more evenly across the day become the dominant influence; weekend travel raises car-pooling for both youth and adults but has no measured effect on transit use, and destination land use shifts toward residential. srcliterature: weekend day loses both commute peaks; purpose mix shifts to social/recreational; carpooling up, transit unchanged (NHTS 2009)CT-RAMP and ActivitySim are weekday models by default with separate weekend estimation where funded; MATSim scenarios build a weekend day from a separate plans file and timetable, as this model does for SAT and SUN.INsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:95 (E.matrix.day_types) and :148 (B.activity.day_purpose_mix) with B.activity.weekend_to_weekday (0.7521, measured) and A.fare.off_peak_all_day_day_types / A.parking.charged_hours_by_day_type per day typeThe board reads a WEEKDAY arm only; day type moves nothing now and becomes live at the scenario stage.
BMobility impairmentPeople with a travel-limiting disability are 8-10% of the population and make fewer trips - about 18.6% fewer overall in the Utah household survey, with the disparity largest on transit (4.21 against 5.71 trips a day) and smallest for driving alone - and they choose differently: a measured shift toward car-pooling, a lower value of travel time, and a transit share that stays low despite a 50% fare concession because access, not price, is the barrier. srcliterature: ~8-10% of the population; ~19% fewer trips; transit trips 4.21 vs 5.71 per day; shift to car passengerActivitySim implementations carry a disability flag into person type where the survey supports it; MATSim scenarios seldom represent it, and this model synthesises the flag without a consumer.PARTIALmobility_impairment_flag synthesised at src/build/build_population.py:262 and written into plans at src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:417; no scoring or availability path in src/java/citysim/ reads it (grep mobility_impairment: no Java match)Walk -11.9%: an unread flag overstates the walk-feasible population at the margin; the literature's ~19% fewer trips for ~8-10% of people is second order against the eight modes past the bar.
CAttraction by purpose (jobs, floorspace, enrolments)The practice is settled on size terms: each destination alternative's utility is a set of impedance terms plus one size function, where the size term is total or industry-specific employment for work, school enrolment for education, and for non-work purposes only the relevant categories - retail employment for shopping, restaurant employment for meals - with households or population for social purposes. Estimation results then show purpose-specific impedance coefficients (e.g. -0.01 business to -0.11 daily shopping per minute in one reported model) around a shared size term. srcliterature: size term = log of a weighted sum of purpose-relevant employment/enrolment/households; impedance coefficients purpose-specific, roughly -0.01 to -0.11 per minute in a reported estimationActivitySim/CT-RAMP estimate the size-term weights per purpose from the survey; MATSim demand builders (as here) declare them and validate against a job distribution.INsrc/build/build_zone_attractions.py:43-45 (D.attraction.job_weight_by_category, purpose_weight) and D.retail.vacancy_rate declared in cities/newcastle/registry/D_landuse.json. Measured this pass on the F29 demand: top work SA2 shares agree with JTW 2011 within 0.5 points, so the attraction side of the commute draw is confirmedLight rail at -45.6% is a CBD-corridor mode; CBD work attraction is measured right, so the light-rail shortfall is not an attraction problem.
CDistance decayThe gravity/spatial-interaction relationship declines with distance, time and cost; the two competing deterrence forms are the power law and the negative exponential, with the negative exponential generally the preferred form in transport application, and the estimated deterrence parameter is sensitive to the spatial arrangement of the study area. srcliterature: negative-exponential deterrence generally preferred over power law; parameter is context- and geometry-sensitive rather than transferableFour-step and gravity models fit a per-purpose deterrence function; ActivitySim replaces it with a logsum-based destination utility; MATSim inherits whatever the demand builder produced.PARTIALsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:465 calibrate_decay solves a per-purpose, per-LGA exponential decay so the realised MEAN distance matches the HTS, and :1992 (B.freight.gravity_beta_per_km) for freight; the short-trip band at :256-257. Measured this pass on the F29 demand: own-LGA commute shares are 7-26 points under JTW 2011 (Cessnock 34.9% vs 60.6%, Lake Macquarie 44.0% vs 54.2%, Maitland 43.9% vs 53.3%, Newcastle 62.4% vs 69.1%, Port Stephens 55.5% vs 62.7%), every neighbour sends 3-7 points too many workers into Newcastle LGA, and none of the 12.8% of residents who work outside the five LGAs exists. The mean is held; the flow structure is not. Previous pass: INHeavy rail +295.1% (the Maitland-line over-boarding is this inter-LGA excess), light_rail -45.6%, car +6.6%. The literature's negative-exponential form is right; a single mean-distance constraint per purpose cannot hold a doubly constrained flow table, which is the practice benchmark.
CConstraints at both ends (capacity)A doubly constrained model preserves both the origin and destination totals from trip generation while a singly constrained one preserves origins only; doubly constrained is the appropriate form where the attraction totals are more reliable than the friction factors, and the standard case for work location, where predicted flows should equal both worker totals and job totals - in activity-based practice this is implemented as shadow pricing on the work and school location choices. srcliterature: no coefficient - a structural choice; doubly constrained (shadow-priced) is standard for work and school, singly constrained for discretionary purposesActivitySim/CT-RAMP shadow-price work and school location to hit zone job and enrolment totals; MATSim demand builders (as here) balance arrivals iteratively.INsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:266 (B.activity.destination_balancing = doubly_constrained) with balancing_passes / balancing_rounds / balancing_tolerance declared in cities/newcastle/registry/B_demand.json; the diagnostic at :733Balancing holds zone arrivals to attraction shares, which is why the top work SA2s match; it constrains where excess heavy_rail (+295.1%) demand can go, not its LGA-to-LGA structure.
CIntra-zonal tripsShort trips are systematically undercounted in travel surveys - the undercount concentrates on short walking, cycling and car trips for shopping and leisure, and every national survey from 1977 to 2022 has undercounted total walk trips by omitting short walks to stops and car parks. More than 80% of walk trips are under 2 km, and walking and cycling behave as substitutes below 2 km. srcliterature: >80% of walk trips are under 2 km; walk trips systematically undercounted in survey targets; walk and bike substitute below 2 kmActivitySim/CT-RAMP handle intrazonal trips with an intrazonal impedance term and micro-zone allocation; MATSim simulates them physically on the real network if the network resolution allows it.PARTIALsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:256-258 - B.activity.short_trip_band_share / short_trip_band_km / short_trip_mean_km declare an observed short-trip band; no intra-zonal impedance term existsWalk -11.9% against a target the literature says is undercounted, bike +157.3%: if walk and bike substitute below 2 km the two errors are one error at the short end.
DDeparture-time profile by purposeDeparture time is a genuine choice, not a fixed profile: Small (1982) tied departure-time choice to a workplace constraint in the utility function, and travellers were willing to shift one to two minutes toward the early side, or one-third to one minute toward the late side, to save one minute of travel time. srcliterature: willingness to shift 1-2 min early, or 1/3-1 min late, per minute of travel time saved (Small 1982)ActivitySim/CT-RAMP model tour departure-time choice by purpose; MATSim mutates departure times each iteration under TimeAllocationMutator and prices the result through the scoring function.PARTIALB.activity.departure_profile (144 assumed numbers, cities/newcastle/registry/B_demand.json) read at src/build/build_activity_chains.py:319 and drawn at :1080-1082; RUN.replanning.time_mutation_range_s = 1800 -> timeAllocationMutator.mutationRange bounds any in-run correction to 30 minutes. Measured this pass on the F29 demand and the F28 gate: F28 pt trips 20.7% in 07:00-09:59 and 13.3% after 19:00 against 42.9% and 0.1% of Opal Hunter bus tap-ons (237,162, weekdays 2016); 8.5% in the 15:00 hour against 31.6%; car trips 21.5% after 20:00 against 6.2% observed. The PT time-of-day profile is inverted. Previous pass: INBus +65.0% is over-carried by adults at hours when the observed bus carries nobody while the school peak that is the observed market is under-generated; heavy_rail +295.1% and light_rail -45.6% read the same shape. The literature's departure-time choice (1-2 min shift per minute saved) is far smaller than the profile error.
DSchedule delay / activity duration preferencesThe schedule-delay cost function is asymmetric: the unit cost of arriving late exceeds the unit cost of arriving early, the disutility falls linearly to zero as arrival approaches the desired time, and Small hypothesises a FIXED penalty component on the late side - arriving late is always bad, however slightly. srcliterature: late-arrival unit cost strictly greater than early; a fixed late penalty on top of the linear termMATSim prices exactly this pair as scoring.lateArrival and scoring.earlyDeparture against an activity's typical and opening/closing times; ActivitySim carries it inside time-of-day choice utilities.PARTIALRUN.scoring.late_arrival_utils_per_h (-18.0) -> scoring.lateArrival and RUN.scoring.early_departure_utils_per_h (0.0) -> scoring.earlyDeparture bound in cities/newcastle/registry/RUN_execution.json; C.scoring.activity_typical_duration_s per activity TYPE; no person-level desired arrival timeSecond order against the eight modes past the bar; it shapes the peak rather than the totals, and the evening excess is a generation error, not a scoring one.
EIn-vehicle time and value of time by purposeThe value of travel time savings is the single best-evidenced coefficient in the field, established by repeated international meta-analysis, and it scales with income: a meta-analysis of 268 income elasticities from 49 studies (1968-2019) puts the income elasticity of VTTS at 0.67 (OLS), 0.77 (WLS) and 0.80 (random effects), below the unity convention still used in appraisal. srcliterature: income elasticity of VTTS approximately 0.7-0.8, below the appraisal convention of 1.0; VTTS itself is purpose-specific by constructionActivitySim/CT-RAMP carry purpose-specific VOT directly in the mode-choice utility; MATSim cannot - it scores per MODE, so a purpose-specific VOT has to be collapsed or pushed into per-person money sensitivity.PARTIALC.vot.by_purpose declares six values (HW 18.6, HE 9.3, HS/HO/HX 15.2, WB 55.4 AUD/h - the HX key reconciled in 9.151) but src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1209-1211 lists 'per-purpose value of time' under not_representable and collapses it to the trip-weighted C.vot.trip_weighted (16.96) at :1077Every money-time trade runs through one VOT: ride -42.8%, bus +65.0% and heavy_rail +295.1% have purpose mixes that differ from the mean, so the collapse biases each differently.
EAccess, egress, wait and transfer time weightsOut-of-vehicle time is valued well above in-vehicle time, and the multipliers are the best-established transferable numbers in the field. Wardman et al. report walk-time multipliers of 1.45 for urban and 1.70 for inter-urban trips and wait-time multipliers of 1.50 and 1.76 respectively; the 2026 update assembles 2,872 multipliers from 606 studies across 52 countries, 1963-2023, covering walk, wait, headway, displacement, reliability and congested time. srcliterature: walk-time multiplier ~1.45 urban (1.70 inter-urban), wait-time multiplier ~1.50 urban (1.76 inter-urban), relative to in-vehicle timeActivitySim/CT-RAMP put these multipliers straight into the mode-choice utility; MATSim expresses them as the difference between a mode's marginalUtilityOfTraveling and the performing rate, plus utilityOfLineSwitch for transfers.INC.time_weights.beta_walk_access / beta_walk_egress / beta_wait (2.0 each) declared in cities/newcastle/registry/C_behaviour.json and translated at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1197-1198 (waiting_pt from beta_wait; utility_of_line_switch from C.transfer.beta_transfer_penalty_min)Declared at 2.0 against the literature's ~1.45 walk / ~1.50 wait, so PT access is priced ABOVE the central tendency - which points away from access as the cause of bus +65.0% and heavy_rail +295.1%.
EFares and money (income-scaled)Public transport demand is fare-inelastic in the short run and considerably more elastic in the long run: the recurring central tendencies are about -0.3 short run and -0.6 to -1.1 long run, with a meta-analysis reporting -0.24 short run against -1.1 long run and Schimek reporting -0.3/-0.7 across a large cross-section of US agencies. srcliterature: short-run PT fare elasticity approximately -0.3 (range -0.24 to -0.4); long-run -0.6 to -1.1ActivitySim/CT-RAMP carry fares as a cost term divided by an income-segmented VOT; MATSim prices fares through a money-event handler and one marginalUtilityOfMoney, optionally per person.INA.fare.* (the published Opal schedule, ~40 observed fields) priced by src/java/citysim/PtFareChargeHandler.java bound at src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:401-403; per-person money sensitivity gated by C.income.representation at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1514With a short-run fare elasticity near -0.3, fares cannot close bus (+65.0%) or heavy_rail (+295.1%); but the income that scales them is drawn wrong (see income row), so the fare channel reaches the wrong people.
EParking cost and search timeUnderpriced parking generates cruising, and cruising is a large share of central-area traffic: studies between 1927 and 2001 found 3.5-14 minutes to find a curb space and 8-74% of traffic cruising, with more recent work above 70%, and search time reaching up to 40% of total travel time. Shoup's operational rule is that a price producing roughly one vacancy in eight (a 12.5% vacancy rate) drives search time to zero. srcliterature: 3.5-14 min search time in congested centres; 8-74% of central traffic cruising; 12.5% vacancy as the price target that removes searchPTV Visum/Aimsun and MATSim's parking contribs simulate search explicitly against facility occupancy; ActivitySim prices parking as a cost term with a separate terminal-time component.INA.parking.search_time_representation = scoring with A.parking.search_min_max scaled by zone density at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:940-949 and switched at :1503; A.parking.price_hr_max / price_threshold_pctile / charged_hours_by_day_type priced by src/java/citysim/ParkingChargeHandler.java (CitysimControler.java:384-386)Car is +6.6%, inside. Raising parking cost pushes car down and the over-supplied modes up; leave it until the eight past the bar are closed.
ETolls and road pricingRoad pricing is demand-elastic at the cordon: estimates for several cities put congestion reductions in the 10 to >30% range if a small share of peak traffic shifts; Singapore's ERP removed ~25,000 peak-hour vehicles and raised average speeds ~20%; a dynamic-pricing corridor simulation moved traffic density by 10-12% across the elasticity range; and the most recent live cordon recorded a 6.3% fall in vehicles entering (about 44,000 a day) against larger projections - real responses are often below the forecast. srcliterature: cordon or corridor pricing cuts affected traffic ~6-30% depending on charge and alternatives; first-year observed responses sit at the low end of forecastsMATSim's roadpricing contrib and Aimsun/Visum toll models price links directly; ActivitySim carries tolls in the cost term with a VOT.OUTgrep -riE 'toll|road_pricing|congestion charg' under src/, cities/newcastle/build and cities/newcastle/registry: no match; the only road money term is parkingNewcastle has no tolled facility in the extent; nothing on the current board. A pricing scenario would need MATSim's roadpricing contrib.
ECar availability and competition for household carsCar availability is the binding constraint on mode, not a preference: the elasticity of active-mode use with respect to car ownership is about -2.6, and the resource logic is that a chain-based mode can only be used if the vehicle is where the traveller left it. Household competition for a limited fleet is what converts a licensed non-driver into a passenger. srcliterature: elasticity of active-mode substitution with respect to car ownership approximately -2.6; car availability dominates person attributes in every reviewed modelMATSim enforces it structurally through chain-based modes in SubtourModeChoice - a mode is offered only if the resource is not conjured out of thin air; ActivitySim/CT-RAMP enforce it through auto-sufficiency segmentation in mode choice.INRUN.mode_choice.consider_car_availability -> subtourModeChoice.considerCarAvailability (cities/newcastle/registry/RUN_execution.json); src/java/citysim/HouseholdCarDepartureHandler.java bound at src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:518-520 so the second driver waits for a car and only for a carThe F28 mechanism that put car inside at +6.6%; the 12,317 refused car legs are the supply for closing ride at -42.8%. Its input is the vehicles draw, which this pass measured as mis-assigned across households.
EPerson attributes: age and sexAge and sex segment travel in direction more than in coefficient: older Australians drive, walk and use taxis and make little use of bicycles, rideshare or public transport; car use declines with age and dependence on transit rises as ability to drive falls; older women are the group most likely to use public transport; the 'gender turnaround' finds young women now travelling more than young men. No transferable coefficient was recovered. src needs researchunknown (direction established: car falls and PT/taxi/walk rise with age; women more PT; no central tendency)ActivitySim/CT-RAMP segment utilities by person type and age band; MATSim carries subpopulation-specific scoring.PARTIALage gates mechanisms - B.population.licence_rate_by_age_band, B.population.bike_min_age (src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:213), B.taxi.min_unaccompanied_age (:287), A.fare.child_min_age / child_max_age / senior_min_age - but no mode utility varies by age or sex; the only person-level scoring variation is income. Measured this pass: income and occupation are drawn independently of age at src/build/build_population.py:307-310 and :358-359Taxi +161.1% with the age gate already in force; age-segmented utilities would mostly move bike (+157.3%) away from the old and young, which the literature's direction supports.
EPerson attributes: incomeIncome raises the value of time sub-proportionally: the meta-analysis of 268 elasticities puts the income elasticity of VTTS at 0.67-0.80, below the unity convention, and income is directly connected to vehicle ownership with higher-income households more inclined to drive alone and less interested in non-motorised modes. srcliterature: income elasticity of VTTS approximately 0.7-0.8 (0.67 OLS, 0.77 WLS, 0.80 RE)ActivitySim/CT-RAMP segment VOT by income band; MATSim's income-dependent scoring sets a per-person marginalUtilityOfMoney as (average income / personal income)^exponent.INC.income.representation = person_marginal_utility_of_money with C.income.exponent = 1.0, consumed at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1514 and by src/java/citysim/IncomeScoringConfigGroup.java bound at src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:206-207; income_band written per person at src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:392 and :419. But the band is drawn at src/build/build_population.py:310 (p_inc from the SA1 total) and :359, independent of age, sex and employment. Measured this pass on the F29 demand: 15-19 year olds >= $1,500/wk 20.6% vs census G17 0.0%; 65-74 18.2% vs 5.9%; 35-44 21.8% vs 38.4%The wiring is live and the data feeding it is wrong: every teenager and pensioner is priced as a prime-age earner and every prime-age earner as a pensioner, so the fare, parking and distance-cost channels reach the wrong people - bus +65.0%, bike +157.3%, walk -11.9%, ride -42.8% (issue #50). The joint tables (G17, G60) are already under data/processed/census/.
EBuilt form: density, diversity, design, distance to transitEwing and Cervero's meta-analysis of the built-environment literature to 2009 is the benchmark: VMT per capita is most strongly related to destination accessibility and secondarily to street-network design; walking relates most strongly to land-use diversity, intersection density and destination counts within walking distance; bus and train use relate equally to proximity to transit and network design, with diversity secondary. Critically, travel is generally INELASTIC with respect to every built-environment measure. srcliterature: all 5D elasticities are inelastic (|e| < 1); destination accessibility dominates VMT, diversity and intersection density dominate walkingActivitySim/CT-RAMP put density, diversity and intersection density into destination and mode utilities as explicit terms; MATSim represents them physically through the network and land use rather than as coefficients.ASCno density, diversity or distance-to-transit term in any mode utility; absorbed into the seven constants in cities/newcastle/registry/C_behaviour.json - C.asc.car_driver (definition, 0) plus C.asc.bus / light_rail / rail / walk / cycle / car_passenger, six held fixed under DECISIONS.md 8.5Because 5D effects are inelastic, folding them into an ASC costs less than it would otherwise; the constants are held fixed so they cannot absorb the misfit.
ETrip purpose and tour complexityMost commute tours are simple: about 80% of US work tours fall into seven dominant patterns and the remaining 20% spread over 106 more complex ones, half of transit work tours are complex, and NHTS defines chaining as at least one intermediate stop between anchors (stays over 30 min); telecommuters make more stops per tour. Discretionary tours are more sensitive to environment than mandatory ones. srcliterature: ~20% of work tours complex (NHTS 2009); half of transit work tours complexCT-RAMP/ActivitySim model stop frequency and location explicitly; MATSim inherits the chain and moves whole subtours.INB.activity.p_intermediate_stop and p_second_stop read at src/build/build_activity_chains.py:164-165; RUN.mode_choice.subtour_behavior -> subtourModeChoice.behavior. Measured this pass on the F29 demand: 20.7% of tours carry an intermediate stop, 79.3% are simple two-leg tours - matching the literature's ~20% complex work toursChain complexity makes car sticky and constrains how much of ride's -42.8% can be recovered by re-moding; the measured share sits where the literature puts it.
ECrowding (seated / standing)Crowding is priced as a time multiplier and the evidence base is large: Wardman and Whelan's synthesis of 208 valuations from 17 British studies over 20 years gives an average seated multiplier of 1.19 and an average standing multiplier of 2.32, with 124 standing observations ranging 0.94-6.05 and 84 seated ranging 1.00-1.78. The standing multiplier is of the same order as the walk and wait multipliers. srcliterature: seated crowding multiplier ~1.19, standing ~2.32 (208 valuations, 17 studies)PTV Visum and Emme price crowding inside transit assignment; MATSim requires an explicit capacity-dependent scoring extension (a contrib) - it is not in core scoring.INERTC.crowding.seated_multiplier (1.0) and standing_multiplier (1.45) reach the C1 file at src/build/build_params.py:101-102, but src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1212-1213 lists 'crowding multipliers (beta_crowding_*): require an explicit capacity-dependent scoring extension, not enabled here' under not_representable; nothing in src/java/citysim/ reads themHeavy rail +295.1%, bus +65.0%: with a standing multiplier of 2.32 unpriced an agent boards a full vehicle at the same utility as an empty one. The seated/standing capacities ARE patched (build_matsim_run_inputs.py:275-278), so the data to price it is in the package.
EReliability and headwayBoth are valued and both are established. The reliability ratio - the value of travel time variability divided by the value of travel time savings, measured against the standard deviation - lies between 0.8 and 1.3 with a value around 1.0 plausible. Headway elasticity of ridership is estimated at -0.263 to -0.277 in disaggregate analysis. srcliterature: reliability ratio 0.8-1.3 (~1.0 central); headway elasticity of ridership approximately -0.26 to -0.28ActivitySim/CT-RAMP include a reliability term where data supports it; MATSim reproduces headway physically from the timetable but has no native reliability disutility.PARTIALheadway is physically simulated from the mapped GTFS (RUN.transit.use_transit, 15 feeds), but C.time_weights.beta_headway (0.5) and beta_reliability (1.3) reach only the C1 parameter file at src/build/build_params.py:99-100 and appear in no emitted configBus +65.0% and heavy_rail +295.1% would both be damped by a reliability penalty at a ratio near 1.0; headway is known per route, so this is cheap.
EComfort, safety, habit, weather, sceneryWeather matters mainly for cycling: its impact on mode choice is marginal overall, with cycling the most affected mode in every spatial setting and walking consistently less sensitive than cycling; a 10% change in cycling volume corresponds to about a 4.0-4.4 K temperature change, ~1 mm of precipitation, or 7.1 m/s of wind gust. Habit is stronger than the rational factors: psychological (rational and habitual) factors influence mode choice more than socio-economic ones, and habit explains behaviour better than rational evaluation. srcliterature: ~4.0-4.4 K temperature change or ~1 mm precipitation per 10% change in cycling volume; habit outweighs rational factors in the reviewed choice modelsNo production city simulator prices habit or weather in the base case; weather appears in research variants of MATSim and SUMO and in bike-demand models, not in appraisal models.OUTgrep -ri 'habit' under src/ and cities/newcastle/: no match; no weather or comfort term in scoring; the only comfort-adjacent mechanism is bike stress (A.bike_stress.*), scored separatelyBike +157.3%: no weather and no habit both bias toward over-cycling; habit is the most plausible unmodelled reason ride is stuck at -42.8%.
EBike: stress (traffic), gradient, e-bikeCyclists trade distance for stress at large, well-measured rates: on average cyclists travel 67% longer to include a cycle path facility, weekend cyclists up to 40% longer, and cyclists accept a 25-38% detour to avoid segments with high near-crash rates. Level of Traffic Stress integrates infrastructure type, road hierarchy, traffic volume and speed limit into one indicator, alongside BCI, BSL and HCM6. Cyclists are highly sensitive to traffic volume where no separate infrastructure exists. srcliterature: detour tolerance 25-38% to avoid high-stress segments; up to 67% longer to include a cycle pathMATSim's bicycle contrib scores infrastructure and gradient on the link; SUMO and Aimsun represent cycling physically without a stress disutility; ActivitySim carries bike-specific impedance in the mode utility.PARTIALA.bike_stress.representation = felt_time with felt_factor_moderate / moderate_high / high stamped at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:779-828 and consumed by src/java/citysim/BikeStressScoring.java and BikeStressDisutility.java (CitysimControler.java:368); A.gradient.bike_uphill_slowdown_per_pct via src/java/citysim/GradientLinkSpeed.java (:351); no e-bike existsBike +157.3%: the literature's 25-38% detour tolerance is the yardstick for the declared felt factors (1.3 / 2.39 / 7.68); an e-bike would point the wrong way.
EWalk: footway width, gradient, crossings, directnessPedestrians are sensitive to network attributes, crossing aids and street/block-face environment, and are willing to divert for better facilities but with limited detour tolerance. Slope directly influences walking effort and route choice, but terrain is perceived as a barrier only when very steep and then only uphill. Distance decay is steep: Walk Score applies no decay within 400 m (5 min) and a 12% decay from 400 to 1,600 m; mean walking access distances to rail stations of 756-805 m are reported for Europe and North America, with Australians willing to walk a little further. srcliterature: no decay under 400 m, ~12% decay 400-1,600 m; mean rail access walk 756-805 m; gradient binds only on steep uphillMATSim can route walk on a real footway network with gradient-adjusted speeds (as here) or teleport it; ActivitySim uses a walk-accessibility skim; SUMO simulates pedestrians physically.INA.active.footway_width_default read at src/build/build_network_layers.py:50; walk gradient via A.gradient.walk_tobler_slope_coeff / walk_tobler_offset through src/java/citysim/GradientLinkSpeed.java; walk routed on the footway network (A.network.pedestrian_excluded_classes); no crossing delayWalk -11.9% with no crossing delay means modelled walking is faster than real walking yet under-produced - the deficit is generation (the short-trip undercount and the evening stacking), not impedance.
ERide: pairing, lifts, detour, wait for driverThe lift is a household object: in the Greater Montreal origin-destination surveys (1987-2003), where passengers named their driver, approximately 70% of all car-passenger trips were intra-household ridesharing, and around 15% of those trips were generated exclusively for the passenger's purpose - a serve trip that creates its own return - with that share rising over the series. Ride-hailing pooling is a separate decision with its own determinants. srcliterature: ~70% of car-passenger trips are household lifts; ~15% of those are pure serve trips generating a returnNo mainstream platform pairs the household lift physically: CT-RAMP/ActivitySim carry car-passenger as a share with an occupancy factor, MATSim scenarios teleport it. Physical pairing is what this project does that the field does not.INB.ride.pairing_enabled / pairing_rule / pairing_window_min / declared_pair_meeting / shared_lift_scope / shared_lift_hash_bucket (0.25 at F29) / shared_lift_priority (longest_first) / wait_for_driver declared in cities/newcastle/registry/B_demand.json and executed by src/java/citysim/RidePairingEngine.java (1,563 lines) bound at src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:448-450Ride -42.8%. The literature now says ~70% of car-passenger trips are household lifts and ~15% of those are pure serve trips - the demand side this model binds. At F28 pairing succeeds (0.9965); placement is the open question the unlaunched F30 arm answers.
ETaxi / rideshare: wait, fleet, refusal, surgeRide-hailing demand is price-sensitive but the estimates are wide: reported price elasticities range from -0.186 (UberX, Houston) through mean point estimates of -0.57 across four US markets to -2.22 in elastic settings, with demand most elastic on daytime weekends and least elastic in off-peak weekday hours. Riders trade price against wait time and are LESS price-sensitive and more wait-sensitive in rush hours and office-dense destinations; fare setting and wait time are simultaneous through network externalities, so a simple elasticity understates the response. srcliterature: ride-hailing price elasticity central estimate about -0.57 (range -0.19 to -2.22); wait-time sensitivity rises in peaksMATSim's DRT/taxi contribs and BEAM simulate the fleet, dispatch and wait physically; ActivitySim represents TNC as a mode with a zonal wait-time skim.PARTIALA.taxi.fleet_representation = finite_fleet with B.taxi.fleet_size (800) / max_wait_min / deadhead_min / vehicle_trips_per_day executed by src/java/citysim/TaxiFleetEngine.java (CitysimControler.java:436-437); C.taxi.wait_min / C.taxi.asc priced at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1153-1157; no surge, no refusal beyond the fleet limitTaxi +161.1%: measured this pass, 21.5% of gate car trips and a fifth of all legs fall after 20:00 when the timetable is empty - taxi is the mode that serves that invented travel. The ASC is swept, never fitted (no target).
EMotorbikeThe motorcycle literature review finds psychological factors - rational and above all habitual - influence mode choice more strongly than socio-economic factors, with habit the better explanation of the two. The recurring determinants are travel time, destination distance, car availability, commuting distance and household income; males prefer cars and motorcycles, higher-income travellers prefer cars, lower-income travellers bicycle and bus. Public-transport quality in the catchment shifts motorcyclists measurably. srcliterature: habit dominates rational factors; car availability, distance and income are the leading observable determinantsAlmost no Western city model simulates motorcycles as a separate physical mode; the Asian ABM literature (and SUMO/Aimsun in motorcycle-dependent cities) treats them as a distinct vehicle class with its own PCE.INB.motorbike.trip_share (0.0038, derived from census G62) read at src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:81 with B.motorbike.carve_resolution, pce and length_m - a distinct physical vehicle classMotorbike +16.1%: outside 10%, inside the stop bar; the carve is anchored on a measured share so the residual is mode choice.
EBus: frequency, stop access, faresBus demand responds to both price and service, and both responses are inelastic in the short run: fare elasticity about -0.3 short run and -0.6 to -1.1 long run, headway elasticity of ridership -0.263 to -0.277. Access is the other half - walk access to stops carries the 1.45 walk multiplier, so stop spacing enters the utility at 1.45 times its clock time. srcliterature: bus fare elasticity ~-0.3 short run; headway elasticity ~-0.26 to -0.28; walk access valued at ~1.45x in-vehicle timeEvery platform in the field simulates bus from a GTFS timetable; the differentiators are whether dwell responds to boardings and whether crowding is priced.INA.fare.bus_* priced by src/java/citysim/PtFareChargeHandler.java; A.transit.bus_capacity_seated (44) / standing (18) patched at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:276; frequency from the mapped GTFSBus +65.0%: fare and headway elasticities near -0.3 cannot explain it. Measured this pass, the observed Hunter bus market is a school-peak market (42.9% of taps 07-10, 31.6% in the 15:00 hour) and the model rides flat into the evening (13.3% after 19:00 vs 0.1%) - the cause is the demand's time shape and the under-generated education tours, before crowding and reliability.
ELight rail: tram priority, dwellTransit signal priority produces large, repeatedly measured delay reductions for the priority vehicle and small costs to cross traffic: 53% and 43% reductions in average bus delay at two studied intersections against 14% and 16% increases in major-phase delay, and in Toronto TSP reduced transit delay 30-40% and travel time 2-6%. Dwell follows the TCQSM linear form - a base plus per-boarding and per-alighting service times; one calibrated model gives a 5.14 s base, 3.48 s per boarding and 1.70 s per alighting, with TCQSM service times of 4.5 s (exact change), 2 s (visual inspection) and 1.75 s (no fare payment). srcliterature: TSP cuts priority-vehicle delay 30-53% and travel time 2-6%; dwell approximately 5.1 s base + 3.5 s per boarding + 1.7 s per alightingAimsun, Vissim and SUMO implement TSP as a controller behaviour; MATSim requires the signals contrib, which this project runs.INA.signals.tsp.mode = green_extension with extension_window_s / detection_distance_m / priority_budget_share / compensation_enabled executed by src/java_signals/citysim/TramPriorityController.java (798 lines); dwell via A.lightrail.dwell_fixed_s (8.0 s) plus the unobtained, swept A.lightrail.dwell_charging_sLight rail -45.6%: TSP runs, so priority is not the cause; the constant dwell means a busy tram is as fast as an empty one. The inverted PT time profile (measured this pass) under-generates the CBD peak the tram serves.
EHeavy rail: capacity, fare, station accessStation access is the binding factor and it is not simply nearest-station: for trips needing an intermodal transfer, riders select the nearest rail station in only 40% of cases; mean walking access distances of 756-805 m are reported, with park-and-ride the dominant access mode at most suburban stations, and faster access modes enlarge the catchment - cycling access can raise train market share by over 10 percentage points at certain access distances. srcliterature: nearest station chosen in only ~40% of intermodal trips; mean walk access 756-805 m; cycle access can add >10 percentage points of train shareEmme/Visum use station-choice and access-mode sub-models; MATSim routes access physically through the transit router's search and extension radii.PARTIALA.transit.rail_capacity_total (146) with seated/standing patched at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:278; A.fare.train_* priced by PtFareChargeHandler.java; access routed by RUN.transit_router.search_radius_m / extension_radius_m / max_beeline_walk_connection_m; grep 'park.and.ride|park_and_ride': no match; no station-choice modelHeavy rail +295.1%, the worst deviation: measured this pass, the excess is an inter-LGA flow excess (own-LGA commute shares 7-26 points low, neighbours over-sending into Newcastle LGA) riding the Maitland line, on top of an unpriced standing multiplier and no park-and-ride access cost.
EFerryFerry ridership is the mode the literature says cannot be forecast from time and cost alone: water-transit riders choose their mode on factors other than travel time and cost, which is why most forecasting models under-perform on it, and the recommended treatment is market segmentation with stated-preference models that separate reaction to time savings by segment - including segments sensitive to travel stress and to environmental preference. Ferry uptake is concentrated among middle-to-high-income workers with a pre-existing preference for ferry-served routes. srcliterature: ferry choice is dominated by attitudinal and segment effects rather than time and cost; uptake concentrated in middle-to-high incomeFerry is normally a hand-segmented mode in four-step practice; no agent-based platform in the survey attempts a behavioural ferry model.PARTIALA.transit.ferry_capacity_total (200) seated 149 / standing 51 patched at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:277; A.fare.ferry_* priced; but src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1165-1174 records that C1 declares NO per-submode constant for ferry, so it inherits the bus ASCFerry -68.7%, the largest under-shoot: the literature says ferry choice is attitudinal, and here ferry carries the bus constant because none is declared - the cheapest single ASC to declare.
ETruck / freight: commodity, time windows, vehicle classAgent-based freight practice models the chain from shipment to tour: SimMobility Freight simulates commodity contracts, logistics and vehicle operation planning and parking decisions fully disaggregately, with a pre-day logistics module covering shipment requirement definition, time-window selection, carrier selection and vehicle operation planning, and ten time-window categories by time of day and duration. Calibration is screenline-based and two-step. srcliterature: full chain is shipment -> time window -> carrier -> vehicle operation plan -> tour; ~10 time-window categories in practice; screenline-based two-step calibrationSimMobility Freight is the reference implementation; MATSim's freight contrib (Schroeder and Liedtke) adds carrier agents to the same mobsim as passengers.PARTIALB.freight.trip_ratio / gravity_beta_per_km (src/build/build_activity_chains.py:1992) / attractor_divisions / pce / max_speed_kmh / length_m and B.truck.resident_trip_share (src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:103) - a gravity-generated truck trip with its own vehicle class; no commodity, time window or carrier tourTruck is level-only (5.96 vs 15.47 network-wide); an understated truck volume makes car (+6.6%) too fast and every alternative less attractive.
EFreight trainThe road-side effect of a freight train is the level-crossing closure, and its length is set by warning-time design as much as by the train: at investigated Australian crossings warning times could be cut by 10-40 s per activation, freight trains run below line speed and so hold the boom longer than passenger trains, and closures at peak produce queue spillback into adjacent signalised intersections; a Brisbane simulation study of seven problem crossings tested treatments on exactly these delays. srcliterature: closure per activation is warning time plus train passage; 10-40 s of the warning time is removable; freight closures are longer than passenger closuresNo agent-based city model simulates freight trains as vehicles; Aimsun/Vissim represent crossings as timed signal closures, which is what this model does with change events.PARTIALA.crossings.representation = change_events with closure_source = schedule_derived, closure_duration_passenger_s (60, literature), closure_duration_s (240) and freight_closures_per_day (0 non-timetabled) built by cities/newcastle/build/build_level_crossings.py; never a mobsim vehicle; the board records 314 modelled against 314 target as a representationNothing directly; it reaches car and bus through the two crossings. The literature's point - freight closures are longer than passenger ones - is what the 240 s vs 60 s split encodes.
FRoute choice and re-routingRoute choice is estimated on GPS-observed routes with path-size logit corrections for overlapping paths; length coefficients turn negative only once infrastructure attributes enter the model, and the adaptive path-size logit resolves the inconsistency of earlier forms. In iterative agent simulation the route set is co-evolved, not enumerated. No transferable share-choosing-shortest-path magnitude was recovered. src needs researchunknown (mechanism established; no central tendency for the shortest-path share)SUMO/Aimsun iterate dynamic user equilibrium; MATSim ReRoute co-evolves the plan set; ActivitySim delegates to assignment.INRUN.routing.network_modes -> routing.networkModes and RUN.replanning.weights (ReRoute 0.15) -> replanning.strategysettings in cities/newcastle/registry/RUN_execution.json; src/java/citysim/GatedSubtourModeChoice.java chains org.matsim.core.replanning.modules.ReRoute after a mode changeRe-routing makes the congestion feedback real; it acts on car (+6.6%) and is not implicated in the eight past the bar.
