FParking search and occupancyCruising for parking is a measured, large phenomenon: 3.5-14 minutes to find a curb space in congested downtowns, 8-74% of the traffic stream cruising (over 70% in recent work), and search time up to 40% of total travel time. A price that holds roughly one vacancy in eight removes the incentive to cruise and drives search time to zero. srcliterature: 3.5-14 min search; 8-74% of central traffic cruising; 12.5% vacancy threshold removes search entirelyMATSim's parking contribs simulate occupancy and search per facility; Aimsun and Vissim model parking search as a route behaviour; ActivitySim uses a terminal-time skim.PARTIALA.parking.search_time_representation = scoring with search_min_max scaled by density at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:940-949 - priced, not simulated; A.parking.occupancy_profile is one declared 24-hour shape applied to every facilityCar is inside at +6.6%, so the priced search is doing its job; absent cruising understates central congestion, one candidate for bus +65.0% and bike +157.3%.
FBoarding, denied boarding and crowdingDenied boarding and in-vehicle crowding are the same evidence base: Wardman and Whelan's 208 valuations give a seated multiplier of 1.19 and a standing multiplier of 2.32, i.e. a minute standing in a crowded vehicle costs more than twice a minute seated in an empty one, and the standing multiplier is of the same order as walk and wait multipliers. srcliterature: standing crowding multiplier ~2.32, seated ~1.19Visum and Emme price crowding inside the transit assignment and can deny boarding at capacity; MATSim denies boarding physically when a vehicle is full but does not price the crowding that precedes it.PARTIALcapacity binds physically because the fleet is patched from published seated+standing figures at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:275-278 (issue 18), but the crowding disutility is not scored (:1212-1213 not_representable)Heavy rail +295.1% and bus +65.0%: agents are refused only at the wall and feel nothing on the approach; PT absorbs demand up to the 146-seat limit.
FRide pairing / matchingPooled matching is measured on platforms, not households: New York taxi pooling reached a 13% match rate on an ordinary day with passengers accepting up to 400 s of delay for up to 49% cost saving, a Chengdu ride-pooling dataset reached an 86.6% match with a 0.12 detour ratio, and driver detours of ~9.2 min are reported when matching riders to drivers with nearby destinations; longer response windows produce better groups and smaller detours. None of this is a household-lift tolerance. src needs researchliterature (platform pooling only): match rates 13-87% by service design; accepted delay ~400 s; detour ratio ~0.12MATSim DRT and BEAM implement insertion-heuristic pooling; no comparable project matches a household lift physically.INsrc/java/citysim/RidePairingEngine.java (1,563 lines) with B.ride.pairing_rule / pairing_window_min / bound_pairing_window_min / shared_lift_scope / shared_lift_priority / shared_lift_hash_bucket / max_passengers_per_vehicle / pickup_dwell_s / remode_unpaired declared in cities/newcastle/registry/B_demand.json; JointRideEngine at CitysimControler.java:488Ride -42.8%: matching succeeds at F28 (pair rate 0.9965); the 0.05 bucket left 94% of 9-15 km tours unserved and F29 raised it to 0.25 with longest-first. The platform literature's match rates (13-87%) are not a household-lift number; that tolerance is still unresearched.
GNetwork detail: lanes, capacity, speed zones, gradientThe capacity defaults have a benchmark: the Highway Capacity Manual base saturation flow is 1,900 passenger cars per hour per lane, with practice reporting 1,800-2,000 pcu/h/lane for a single lane and arterial capacity estimated from 1,900 per lane; Austroads capacity guidance carries the same base. Downscaled agent simulations then scale flow capacity with the sample and storage a little higher at small samples. srcliterature: base saturation flow 1,900 pc/h/lane (HCM), 1,800-2,000 in practice; flow capacity scaled by sample shareSUMO and Aimsun take lanes and capacity from the network build; MATSim takes them from the OSM conversion with per-class defaults and scales by sample.INA.road.lanes_default, A.road.speed_default (measured from observed speed zones), A.road.capacity_default (assumed convention, motorway 2000 / trunk 1800 / primary 1600) and the four *_unknown_class fallbacks declared 9.151 in cities/newcastle/registry/A_supply.json; A.gradient.representation = link_speed consumed by src/java/citysim/GradientLinkSpeed.java (src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1689)Capacity decides how much congestion car (+6.6%) feels. The literature's 1,900 pc/h/lane base sits above the declared primary/secondary convention, so if anything the model is slightly congestion-heavy.
GSignals: adaptive control and transit priorityAdaptive control and transit signal priority are separately measured and both are material: SCATS evaluations report PM weekday travel-time reductions averaging 3.9% and weekend 1.9%, with adaptive strategies up to 29% in the widest reported range and 6-11% in Toronto; TSP reduces transit delay 30-40% and transit travel time 2-6%, with a measured 53% and 43% cut in average bus delay at two studied intersections against 14-16% increases in major-phase delay. srcliterature: SCATS travel-time savings ~2-11% typical; TSP transit delay -30 to -53%, transit travel time -2 to -6%Vissim, Aimsun and SUMO implement adaptive control and TSP as controller logic; MATSim requires the signals contrib, which few published scenarios run.INA.signals.representation = explicit_signals with A.signals.control_regime = scats_adaptive and A.signals.scats.target_degree_saturation / cycle_step_s / min_cycle_s / max_cycle_s / ds_deadband / ds_smoothing executed by src/java_signals/citysim/ScatsSignalController.java (918 lines); tram priority by TramPriorityController.java (798 lines). The F30 launch was refused because the signals stack was not built (runs table), and the stack is bootstrapped nowLight rail -45.6% with TSP running: signals are not the light-rail cause; one of the few places the model is ahead of the field.
GTransit operations: dwell, headway, capacityDwell is a linear function of passenger flow, not a constant: TCQSM estimates it from alighting and boarding counts, a per-passenger service time and a door-opening constant, with service times of 4.5 s (exact change into the farebox), 2 s (visual inspection) and 1.75 s (no fare payment); a calibrated model gives a 5.14 s base plus 3.48 s per boarding and 1.70 s per alighting, with small diminishing marginal effects. srcliterature: dwell approximately 5.1 s base + 3.5 s per boarding + 1.7 s per alighting; fare-payment method moves per-passenger service time from 1.75 s to 4.5 sVisum and Emme use load-dependent dwell in transit assignment; MATSim's transit engine applies a fixed or schedule-derived dwell unless a contrib replaces it.PARTIALdwell is declared as constants - A.lightrail.dwell_fixed_s (8.0), A.transit.era1_station_dwell_s (30.0), E.s1.shuttle_dwell_s, E.s3.brt_dwell_s - with no boardings term; headway and capacity are real (mapped GTFS, published seated/standing patch at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:275-278)Heavy rail +295.1%, bus +65.0%, light rail -45.6% are all decided at the stop: with a constant dwell a bus carrying 65% too many runs exactly on time. The boarding counts to drive a TCQSM dwell exist in the events file.
GQueueing model and passingMATSim's default link is a spatial FIFO queue with two parameters, flow capacity and storage capacity, and no intra-link interaction; the passing-queue extension lets faster vehicles overtake slower ones within a link so that, when walking and cycling are simulated on the road, pedestrians and cyclists do not block cars in the queue - the AToM Melbourne model documents this as the required setting for a multimodal network. srcliterature: no coefficient - a discipline choice; FIFO blocks a queue behind the slowest agent, PassingQ does notMATSim (FIFO by default, PassingQ or holes optionally); SUMO and Aimsun use car-following models where passing is physical.INRUN.qsim.link_dynamics = PassingQ -> qsim.linkDynamics (cities/newcastle/registry/RUN_execution.json, DECISIONS.md 9.59); walk PCE 0.0 and bike PCE 0.2 (B.walk.pce, B.bike.pce)Already priced into the board: under FIFO walk and bike would have throttled car on shared links.
GExternal and through trafficExternal and through trips are surveyed at the cordon: the object of an external cordon survey is the trips that originate outside the region and end inside it or pass through, and regional practice forecasts them with Fratar or gravity models calibrated on cordon counts and updated from census journey-to-work flows; Australian guidance (ATAP) treats the external zone system as part of model design. No transferable through-share magnitude was found - it is a property of the cordon geometry. src needs researchunknown (no transferable through-traffic share; cordon-specific by construction)Every regional model carries external stations with cordon-count-calibrated I-E, E-I and E-E trips; MATSim scenarios add boundary agents in the demand builder.PARTIALB.external.through_share read at src/build/build_activity_chains.py:1977 with commute_share_to_core, interaction_rate (:1948, derived from JTW 2011), cordon_road_classes and agent_profile; external_agents at :2336 draws destinations over the CORE zones only - an inbound tier with no outbound resident commuting. Measured this pass on the F29 demand: 29,603 of 231,168 employed residents (12.8%; 26.3% of Cessnock's) work outside the five LGAs in JTW 2011 and the synthetic count is 0. Previous pass: INThose missing out-of-region commuters are drawn to in-region jobs instead, part of the inter-LGA excess that rides heavy_rail (+295.1%) and adds to car (+6.6%); the boundary counts stay biased and calibrate.py still refuses to fit them.
GIncidents and weatherWeather is a measured share of non-recurring delay and a measured speed effect: snow, ice and fog alone cause 15% of non-recurring delay (FHWA), a light rain raises travel-time delay 12-20%, wet pavement cuts arterial speeds 10-25% and light rain cuts freeway speed 2-13%, heavy rain reduces capacity through visibility; incidents and work zones together are about 35% of non-recurring congestion, and rain compounds an incident's speed effect. The weather effect on cycling volume (4.0-4.4 K per 10%) is on the mode-choice row. srcliterature: light rain +12-20% delay, arterial speed -10 to -25% on wet pavement; weather ~15% and incidents ~35% of non-recurring delayNo mainstream city model represents incidents or weather in a base case; SUMO and Aimsun carry them as scenario overlays (capacity and speed factors).OUTgrep -riE 'weather|rainfall|incident' under src/ and cities/newcastle/registry matches only unrelated tokens; every simulated day is identicalBike +157.3%: a perpetually fine day is a systematic upward bias on cycling of the order the literature quantifies.
HUtility form (Charypar-Nagel scoring)MATSim's scoring is the Charypar-Nagel form: plan utility is the sum of activity utilities plus travel disutilities, with activity utility beta_dur * t_typ * ln(t_dur / t_0) - marginal utility of duration against a typical duration and a minimal duration below which utility is negative - and leg score built from a mode constant, a marginal disutility of travel duration, and a marginal disutility of distance. Under iteration the population's average plan score stabilises at a point where individuals cannot unilaterally improve. srcliterature: activity utility is logarithmic in duration against a typical duration; leg score is linear in time and distance plus a mode constantMATSim and its derivatives (eqasim, BEAM) score Charypar-Nagel; ActivitySim/CT-RAMP use nested-logit utilities instead, which is a different object - a nest coefficient has no MATSim equivalent.INC.scoring.performing_utils_per_h, marginal_utility_of_money, monetary_distance_rate, activity_typical_duration_s, activity_minimal_duration_s, mode_constant, marginal_utility_of_traveling, waiting_pt and utility_of_line_switch declared in cities/newcastle/registry/C_behaviour.json and emitted at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1181-1199; RUN.scoring.brain_exp_beta -> scoring.BrainExpBetaThe form every deviation is expressed in; the reason the nest coefficients and per-purpose VOT are lost in translation (9.3).
HHeterogeneity / value-of-time segmentsHeterogeneity in the value of time is real and income-driven, with an income elasticity of VTTS of about 0.67-0.80 - below the unity convention. MATSim's own agent-heterogeneity work treats per-agent parameter variation as a first-class scenario feature rather than an extension. srcliterature: income elasticity of VTTS ~0.7-0.8; heterogeneity is income-led rather than idiosyncraticActivitySim/CT-RAMP segment VOT into income bands inside the utility; MATSim varies marginalUtilityOfMoney per person or defines subpopulation-specific scoring parameters.PARTIALincome heterogeneity live (C.income.representation, src/java/citysim/IncomeScoringConfigGroup.java); RUN.replanning.subpopulations = person/external/freight; the TIME side is one trip-weighted VOT (src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1077)Segments differ on money and not on time; with the income draw mis-assigned by age (measured this pass) the one live axis is also pointed at the wrong people.
HChoice-set generation and mode availabilityThe choice set in an agent-based model is generated, not enumerated: MATSim's SubtourModeChoice changes the mode of all legs of one randomly chosen subtour to a randomly chosen alternative, and offers a mode only where the choice would not require a resource to appear out of thin air - chain-based modes assume one resource per mode, initially at home. The discrete-mode-choice contrib exists for scenarios needing an explicit, estimable choice model instead. srcliterature: subtour-level mode changes with chain-based resource constraints; explicit choice-set generation available only through the discrete-mode-choice contribActivitySim/CT-RAMP enumerate the alternatives and evaluate a nested logit; MATSim searches co-evolutionarily; eqasim bridges the two by putting a discrete choice model inside MATSim.INRUN.mode_choice.modes -> subtourModeChoice.modes and chain_based_modes; src/java/citysim/GatedSubtourModeChoice.java (572 lines) bound at src/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:271 with ModeAvailabilityConfigGroup and AvailabilityModesCalculator (:261)Every mode's ceiling is set here; taxi at +161.1% is offered to too many agents at too many hours.
HLearning, replanning, plan memory, innovation switch-offThe distinction that governs convergence: while innovation is switched on - new routes, new times - the result is NOT truly stationary; if innovation is switched off the process is stationary but limited to the plans each agent holds at that moment. The plan set is the agent's choice set, and MATSim's recommended control is fractionOfIterationsToDisableInnovation rather than a per-strategy disable iteration. srcliterature: no stationarity while innovation runs; stationarity after switch-off but restricted to the existing plan setMATSim, eqasim and BEAM all use an innovation-off tail; ActivitySim has no equivalent because it does not iterate agents against each other in the same way.INRUN.replanning.max_agent_plan_memory (8), fraction_to_disable_innovation (0.8), weights, RUN.scoring.brain_exp_beta and learning_rate bound in cities/newcastle/registry/RUN_execution.jsonWhy no reading on the board is a result: every arm since F4 stopped at an iteration-100 gate before the cutoff.
HLLM-driven agentsThe 2025 evidence is that LLM agents can reproduce realistic travel behaviour and system-level dynamics in morning-commute settings and can serve as the agent model inside a multi-agent simulation such as MATSim; alignment techniques - few-shot learning and travel-behaviour persona loading - materially improve mode-choice accuracy and can surpass traditional discrete choice models where domain knowledge is supplied. LLM agents partially replicate human route-switching behaviour against laboratory data. The stated blocker is computational: scaling to population level. srcliterature: persona-aligned LLM agents match or exceed discrete choice models on mode-choice prediction in reported studies; population-scale deployment remains computationally infeasibleNo production city twin runs LLM agents; the work is research-stage, mostly as an agent model plugged into MATSim or as a standalone route-choice study.OUTgrep -riE 'LLM|language model' under src/ matches only unrelated tokens (e.g. 'fuLLMoon'-style substrings in comments); agents are scored by the Charypar-Nagel functionNothing on the current board; the literature's scaling caveat rules it out at 25% of a 600,000-person region.
ITargets and the validation ladderPractice has explicit numeric acceptance criteria: transit validation standards of about +/-9% for regional estimated-over-observed boardings and +/-20% for transit screenlines, and MDOT screenline/cutline targets of 5% and 10% for percent difference between observed and estimated volumes. The manual also warns that counts themselves vary by 10% or more from daily and seasonal variation, and recommends at least one midweek 24-hour count every two years. srcliterature: +/-9% regional transit boardings, +/-20% transit screenlines, 5%/10% screenline/cutline volume targets; count data itself carries >=10% variabilityEvery MPO model in the US validates against this manual; MATSim scenarios in the literature typically report link-count fits and rarely per-mode ridership for every mode.INsrc/calibrate/fit.py scores calibration targets with CAL.gate.stop_deviation_pct (20) and CAL.gate.pass_deviation_pct (10) in cities/newcastle/registry/CAL_calibration.json; src/analyse/build_status_board.py generates the twelve-mode board from a named run at a named iterationAhead of the field: every mode individually inside 10% is stricter than FHWA's +/-9% regional boardings; the board honestly reports 1 of 12 inside.
IHoldout enforcementValidation compares the model against information other than that used to estimate it; the common practice is a random split into estimation and holdout samples at 80/20 or 75/25, with out-of-sample performance indices computed on the withheld part, and MPO guidance asks for calibration and validation at every model step. What the guidance does not describe is enforcement - no surveyed practice makes the holdout unreadable by construction. srcliterature: 80/20 or 75/25 estimation/holdout splits; validation on data not used in estimationStandard in estimation of choice models; conventional rather than enforced in MPO validation; not a feature of MATSim or ActivitySim tooling.INsrc/calibrate/fit.py:6-8 - load_targets() filters split == 'calibration' at read time and raises if anything else survives; src/calibrate/calibrate.py:5-11 adds an independent second check; the 67/143 split is pre-registered (DECISIONS.md 12)Nothing on the current board by design; structural enforcement is stronger than the 80/20 convention the literature describes.
IConvergence criterionConvergence in an iterative agent model has a precise meaning and a precise trap: the process is not stationary while innovation runs, and is stationary after switch-off only within the plans agents already hold. Empirically, between-seed variation in link loads dominates the variation between the last two iterations within one seed, so a within-run stability test alone is not evidence of convergence. srcliterature: between-seed variation of link loads exceeds last-two-iteration within-seed variationMATSim practice reads score and mode-share stability after the innovation cutoff; ActivitySim has no iterative convergence criterion of this kind.INRUN.relaxation.drift_tolerance_pp (0.5) and settle_margin_iterations (10) read at src/analyse/summarise_run.py:75-85 and applied in relaxation() at :144-171Exists and has never fired - no arm since F4 has reached its cutoff; GOAL.md's <=250 requirement is unmeasured, and the literature says a within-run drift test is necessary, not sufficient.
IReplication across seeds / run-to-run noiseRandom seeds move agent-based results materially: across 100 seeds of one MATSim scenario, relative errors of up to 10% occur even on links with large volumes, and the variation between seeds largely dominates the variation between the two last iterations within a seed. Aggregate travel times are robust after one iteration, but disaggregate results needed about 31 simulations on average to reach a robust mean. srcliterature: up to 10% relative link-volume error across seeds; ~31 replications for a robust disaggregate mean; between-seed >> within-seed variationAimsun and Vissim require multiple seeded replications as standard practice; most published MATSim scenarios report a single seed, which is the field's most common methodological weakness.PARTIALE.replication.n_replications (30) read at cities/newcastle/build/build_scenario_configs.py:40 and enforced by tests/check_package.py:117; RUN.machine.seed -> global.randomSeed; overlay cities/newcastle/overlays/runs/phys1000_arm_b_25pct.json exists; no replication pair has completedDecides whether any deviation is signal: with a ~10% literature noise floor, walk -11.9% and motorbike +16.1% may be noise, and car +6.6% cannot be called inside with confidence.
ISensitivity sweepsThe recommended method for agent-based models is variance-based global sensitivity analysis: because ABMs are non-linear, Sobol' indices decompose the output variance into first-order and total contributions of each parameter and its interactions, sampled with Sobol' sequences over the input space; one-at-a-time sweeps are the local, linear special case and miss interactions. srcliterature: no coefficient - a method; Sobol' total-order indices over a Sobol'-sequence sample, typically hundreds to thousands of runsPublished MATSim and SUMO studies mostly do one-at-a-time sweeps of a few parameters; the ABM literature recommends Sobol' indices as routine practice.PARTIALcities/newcastle/params/C1_sensitivity_sweep_grid.csv written by src/build/build_params.py:267 from C.transfer.penalty_sweep_grid (:116) and A.lightrail.dwell_sweep_grid (:172); no arm has executed a sweep pointThe charging-dwell sweep bears on light rail at -45.6% and has never run; the literature's Sobol' method is a step beyond the one-at-a-time grid.
IASC calibration methodAn alternative-specific constant is the net average effect of the variables the utility omits, and calibration adjusts it iteratively - run, compare modelled to observed mode shares, move the constants, repeat until the fit is acceptable. UK TAG supplementary guidance on bespoke mode choice models is the formal statement; the risk it names is that constants absorb specification error and any new alternative has no constant to inherit. srcliterature: no coefficient - an iterative adjustment to observed shares; the constant is the mean of the omitted variablesActivitySim/CT-RAMP calibrate ASCs to survey shares as a routine final step; MATSim scenarios adjust mode constants by hand or, as here, declare them fixed so misfit stays visible.ASCsix of seven constants in cities/newcastle/registry/C_behaviour.json carry a held_fixed rule (DECISIONS.md 8.5); src/calibrate/calibrate.py:14-17 makes them unreachable from the loop by construction; C.asc.car_passenger's solved value comes from src/calibrate/solve_asc_ride.pyHolding the constants fixed is why the misfits stay visible: with ASCs free, heavy rail's +295.1% would vanish into asc_rail.
JPopulation synthesisPopulation synthesis is the required input to any agent model because individual-level attributes for the whole population do not exist; the established techniques are iterative proportional fitting, iterative proportional updating, combinatorial optimisation, and Markov- and fitness-based synthesis. There is no clear guideline on choosing among them, and integer conversion and the zero-cell problem are the outstanding issues. srcliterature: IPF/IPU/combinatorial optimisation/Markov the established families; no consensus on choice; integer conversion and zero cells the open problemsActivitySim ships PopulationSim; MATSim scenarios use eqasim's synthesiser or a bespoke one; every platform in the survey treats the synthetic population as an input rather than a modelled object.PARTIALsrc/build/build_population.py places households on SA1 marginals (:281) with age-sex (:331), labour force and education per SA1 (:305-306), measured licence rates (:62); but occupation and income are drawn from the SA1 TOTALS at :307-310 and :358-359 independent of age, sex and employment, and vehicles at :296/:322 independent of size, composition and income. Measured this pass on the F29 demand (612,634 persons): 15-19 year olds earning >= $1,500/wk 20.6% vs G17 0.0%, 65-74 18.2% vs 5.9%; clerical 14.4-15.8% in every age band; car-less households 36.0% lone-person vs 65.3% nationally. The joint tables G17 and G60 are already under data/processed/census/. Previous pass: INThe synthetic population is marginal-correct and joint-wrong. Because income now scales every person's marginal utility of money and the vehicle roster decides who waits for a car, the fare, parking, distance-cost and car-availability channels all reach the wrong people: bus +65.0%, bike +157.3%, walk -11.9%, ride -42.8% (issue #50). The literature's IPF/IPU families exist precisely to hold these joints.
JTravel survey (HTS) weighting and vintageHousehold travel survey estimates are produced on a rolling basis from multiple pooled years and weighted to the ABS Estimated Resident Population for the collection year - so an HTS figure is a multi-year average, not a single-year observation. The survey's known systematic weakness is the undercount of short walk trips: every national survey from 1977 to 2022 has undercounted total walk trips by omitting short walks to stops and car parks. srcliterature: HTS estimates are rolling multi-year pooled and ERP-weighted; walk trips systematically undercounted in every survey series examinedEvery activity-based model in the field calibrates against an HTS of this kind; the vintage-versus-base-year mismatch is universal and rarely stated.PARTIALB.activity.hts_rate_per_person_day (3.473) and B.activity.day_purpose_mix declared from the HTS; mode-share targets read through src/analyse/extract_metrics.py:8 on the published MODE_SHARE definition; src/build/hts_purpose.py holds the one purpose map (9.151); no weighting or vintage adjustment. Measured this pass: HW 18.6% of synthetic legs vs 14.0% HTS commute, HE 5.7% vs 9.6%Walk -11.9% against an undercounted target; the purpose shares the HTS publishes are now the measured yardstick the demand misses on commute and education.
JSmartcard (Opal) and station countsSmartcard data is the standard calibration source for transit and it supports high-quality validation - agent-based models calibrated on it reach R-squared around 0.85 on on-board bus volumes - but it is structurally incomplete: most datasets capture only entry and egress points with no routing information, so trip-chaining is required to infer alighting stops and identify transfers. srcliterature: smartcard-calibrated transit ABMs reach R^2 ~0.85 on on-board volumes; alighting and transfers must be inferred by trip-chainingVisum, Emme and MATSim scenarios all calibrate PT to smartcard boardings where available; per-station validation for every mode is uncommon.INCAL.pt_split.window_months / station_scope / break_ratio / lr_observed_stop_share and CAL.pt.weekday_factor / censored_cell_value / censored_share_max declared in cities/newcastle/registry/CAL_calibration.json; B.opal.journey_linked unobtained; rail and tram targets from disclosed boardings (DECISIONS.md 9.130). The 2016 Opal tap-time files under data/raw/opal/ were used this pass to measure the PT time profile, not yet as a targetHeavy rail +295.1% is scored on the smartcard basis; the same data's time-of-day shape (measured this pass) is the sharpest unfitted observation in the package.
JRoad countsTraffic counts are not a fixed truth: counts alone vary by 10% or more from daily and seasonal variation, and FHWA recommends a minimum of one midweek 24-hour count at least every two years to obtain a typical ADT estimate. Validation percentages are therefore reported by functional class and against screenlines rather than link by link. srcliterature: >=10% intrinsic variability in count data; validation reported by functional class and screenline, not per linkEvery four-step and ABM practice validates on counts; MATSim scenarios in the literature report link-count scatter as the primary validation.INB.counts.heavy_vehicle_share and CAL.truck.count_year_from declared; src/analyse/map_count_stations.py matches stations and cities/newcastle/params/C3_count_comparison.json holds the comparison; src/calibrate/calibrate.py:26-30 refuses to optimise against counts. The light-vehicle hourly profile (data/processed/observed/light_hourly_profile.csv, 551 station-years) was used this pass to measure the departure shapeCounts constrain truck (level only) more than any resident mode; both sides of the comparison changed basis in 9.150.
JGTFS and OSM completenessOpenStreetMap road completeness is about 83% globally (Barrington-Leigh and Millard-Ball 2017) and highest in cities; a 41,000 km Australian road network study finds OSM navigation performance correlates strongly with data quality, which itself tracks city population and ICT infrastructure. GTFS is the interoperable timetable format because timetables change too often for OSM; the join between the two (pt2matsim here) is the recurring failure point. srcliterature: OSM roads ~83% complete globally, higher in cities; Australian OSM quality tracks population and ICTpt2matsim, OpenTripPlanner and UrbanAccess join GTFS to OSM; validators (gtfs-validator) check feed integrity but not map completeness.PARTIALharvest extent boundary-derived (A.osm.harvest_margin_m = 5,000 m, harvest_tile_deg, harvest_attempts); 15 feeds mapped, 0 unmapped stops (DECISIONS.md 3.5, 9.35); the four *_unknown_class fallbacks declared 9.151; pt2matsim mapping non-reproducible (~18% of route link sequences)The ~18% non-reproducible sequences put a floor under how precisely light rail (-45.6%) and heavy rail (+295.1%) can be attributed to any single change.
KSample fraction and scaling rulesDownscaling has measured limits: simulations at 25% or higher of the traveller population preserve all major urban traffic statistics, while below 10% even average statistics become unreliable, with scores and travel times the first to degrade. The scaling rule is that flowCapacityFactor follows the sample share and storageCapacityFactor is set a little higher at samples of 10% or below; in one published scenario a 1% population needed a 2% flow capacity factor to reproduce the observed travel-distance distribution. srcliterature: >=25% preserves all major traffic statistics; below 10% even averages are unreliable; storage capacity factor set above flow at small samplesMATSim, SUMO and BEAM all scale link capacities with the sample; the field's usual practice is 1-10%, and 25% is at the high end of published scenarios.INRUN.sample.fraction with flow_capacity_factor derived = fraction (src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1279-1280), storage_capacity_exponent / factor, transit_capacity_scaling and transit_capacity_floor; RUN.sample.unit = householdRuns at 25%, the literature's threshold that preserves all major traffic statistics; no deviation can be dismissed as sampling.
KIteration count and costThere is no standard iteration count: the process is run until the average population score stabilises, simple car-only scenarios converge fast, complex multimodal ones sometimes do not converge by iteration 100, one published scenario converged at iteration 164 and others run 500; because the simulation is stochastic, deterministic convergence criteria do not apply. srcliterature: 100-500 iterations in published scenarios; one converged at 164; no multimodal twelve-mode benchmarkPublished MATSim scenarios commonly run 100-500 iterations with an innovation-off tail; eqasim and BEAM likewise.INRUN.controler.last_iteration (1000, measured), RUN.gate.interval_iterations (100), RUN.monitor.pace_band_s ([217, 253] measured); the F28 arm ran at a median 260 s an iteration, ~22 h for 300The binding constraint on the programme: every arm since F4 stopped at 100, so the board reads an unstationary process; the literature's 100-500 range brackets the 300-iteration arm design.
KReproducibility of a runRun-to-run reproducibility is not achievable by fixing a seed alone in this class of model: across 100 seeds relative errors up to 10% occur on high-volume links, and between-seed variation dominates the last-two-iteration within-seed variation. Reporting a single seeded run is therefore reporting one draw from a distribution. srcliterature: up to 10% relative link-volume error across seeds; between-seed variation dominates within-seedAimsun and Vissim require multiple replications; most published MATSim scenarios report one seed and do not state the noise floor.PARTIALinputs fully seeded (B.seed.master = 20260810, RUN.machine.seed, blake2b household hashing at src/build/build_activity_chains.py:247, every derived file hashed in cities/newcastle/data/MANIFEST.csv - 512 files, source 508 of 512 after 9.151); the run side is not: pt2matsim mapping differs ~18% between identical builds and MATSim runs are not bit-reproducibleInput reproducibility is ahead of the field; output reproducibility is not achievable, which is why no deviation should be quoted without the error bar the project has not measured.

A clean tree, an unmerged branch and an arm at work

The tree is clean. The branch carries four commits past origin/main and no pull request is open: they close issues #147–#151, order the escort listener's seeded draw, make the toolchain gate refuse a checkout that cannot launch, and record the refused launch on the board. The F30 arm 20260907T150816_300it_25pct was launched at 15:08 (25 %, 300 iterations, 16 threads, 40 g heap) and is running; its record in _progress.json is what the performance pass reads. The board's scoreboard and runs blocks are stale against it, which is the one failing gate check. Nothing here was built on, committed or reverted by this report.

appendix

How this report was made, and how to make it again

Run the three collectors under .claude/skills/project-report/scripts/ into a scratch directory, launch the six phase reviewers with the briefs in the skill, make the demand measurements with the scripts recorded in this session (a B2 pass for departure hours, chaining and commute flows; a B1 pass for income by age and car-less households; a trips-table pass for modes by hour; a JTW pass for own-LGA shares), then run the assembler build_report.py with the stamp. Every table above is rendered from the JSON embedded at the end of this file.

Verification performed on this report

Twelve cited file:lines were re-read by the writer before publishing (calibrate.py:486-491, extract_legacy_constants.py:50-54, build_corridor_layers.py:122-128, results_store.py:377-381, run_signal_probes.py:72-91, build_manifest.py:257-263 and :362-377, build_charging_dwell_offsets.py:112, RidePairingEngine.java:1099-1109, measure_mode_constraints.py:51-57, doc_shape.json:58, build_population.py:296-310) and every one read as cited. Five rows searched this pass were re-fetched: the Deep Activity Model abstract and the SUMO downloads page confirmed their cells; the MWCOG Gen3 report and the Dhaka thesis PDFs resolved (4.5 MB and 7 MB) though the fetcher could not summarise them; BEAM's LICENSE.md path returned 404 while the row cites the repository licence tab. The reused library rows were verified by inspection of their source URL and last-verified date. The demand-synthesis measurements were made by the writer with the scripts named in the appendix and are reproducible from the package.

Colour and accessibility

The categorical palette (six hues, light and dark steps) passes the dataviz validator's six checks in both themes; severity and status use the reserved status colours with a text label beside every mark; every chart carries a title, one axis and a caption naming its source.
